TUZA’S CONJECTURE FOR GRAPHS OF MAXIMUM DEGREE AT
                                                                MOST SEVEN

                                                                                       ANISH GUPTA


                                                  Abstract. Tuza conjectured that every finite simple graph G satisfies τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G),
                                                  where ν(G) is the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles and τ (G) is the
                                                  minimum number of edges whose deletion makes G triangle-free. Puleo proved the conjec-
                                                  ture for every graph of maximum average degree less than 7; this covers maximum degree
                                                  at most 6 but no 7-regular graph. We prove the conjecture for maximum degree at most 7.
                                                     The proof uses Puleo’s reducible-set framework. At average degree seven his discharging
                                                  step no longer forces a reducible configuration. In a minimal 7-regular counterexample
                                                  every vertex link is a connected seven-vertex graph outside the weak Kőnig–Egerváry class.
                                                  An exhaustive census of such links supplies, at every vertex, an incident edge lying in four,
                                                  five or six triangles. We prove that its endpoints form a reducible pair: codegrees five

                                                  and six use a packing-and-cover template and Fano-plane witnesses, while codegree four
                                                  uses an explicit catalogue of 1,144 machine-checked local certificates. We do not provide
                                                  a human-readable proof of that catalogue; the certificates and their verifiers accompany

                                                                                    1. Introduction
                                             All graphs in this paper are finite, simple and undirected. A triangle packing of a graph
                                          G is a set of triangles of G that are pairwise edge-disjoint; distinct triangles of a packing
                                          may share vertices. We write ν(G) for the largest size of a triangle packing. A triangle
                                          transversal (or triangle edge cover) is a set Y ⊆ E(G) such that G − Y is triangle-free, and
                                          τ (G) is the smallest size of one. Every transversal meets each member of an edge-disjoint
                                          packing, and those meetings use distinct edges, so ν(G) ≤ τ (G). Conversely, deleting all
                                          three edges of every triangle in a maximum packing leaves no triangle: a surviving triangle
                                          would be edge-disjoint from the packing and could be added to it. Thus τ (G) ≤ 3ν(G).
                                          Conjecture 1.1 (Tuza [9, 10]). Every graph G satisfies τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G).
                                             Tuza’s original formulation gives the conjecture a second interpretation [9]. Let α1 (G)
                                          be the maximum number of edges in a triangle-free subgraph of G, and let ρ0 (G) be the
                                          minimum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles and single edges whose union is E(G).
                                          Then α1 (G) = |E(G)| − τ (G) and ρ0 (G) = |E(G)| − 2ν(G), so ρ0 (G) ≤ α1 (G) is equivalent
                                          to Tuza’s conjecture.
                                             The conjecture is open. Haxell proved the universal bound τ (G) ≤ (66/23) ν(G) [4].
                                          Among the classes for which the conjecture is known are planar graphs (Tuza [10]); triangle-
                                          3-colourable graphs, a class containing all 4-colourable graphs (Aparna Lakshmanan, Bujtás
                                          and Tuza [1]); and K5 -free chordal graphs (Tuza [10, Proposition 3(b)]). Krivelevich proved
                                          the conjecture for graphs with no subdivision of K3,3 [6]. Botler, Fernandes and Gutiérrez
                                          strengthened the last result to K8 -free chordal graphs by proving the conjecture for graphs
                                          of treewidth at most six; they also proved τ ≤ 32 ν for every planar triangulation other
                                          than K4 [2]. Kahn and Park proved that for every edge-probability function p = p(n), the

for the maximum average degree of G. For the empty graph we set mad(∅) = 0.
Theorem 1.2 (Puleo [8, Theorem 1.2]). If mad(G) < 7, then τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G).
   The hypothesis of Theorem 1.2 is strict, and the strictness has a sharp consequence for
bounded-degree graphs. If ∆(G) ≤ 6 then every subgraph has average degree at most
6, so mad(G) ≤ 6 < 7 and Theorem 1.2 applies. If, on the other hand, G is 7-regular,
then mad(G) = 7 and Theorem 1.2 says nothing at all about G. The 7-regular graphs are
therefore exactly what separates “maximum degree at most six”, which is covered, from
“maximum degree at most seven”, which is not. Our main theorem closes that gap.
   There is an apparent one-edge shortcut, but it misses the conjectured bound by exactly
the amount that matters. If G is connected and 7-regular and e ∈ E(G), then G − e is a
proper subgraph, so mad(G − e) < 7 by Lemma 3.1(b). Puleo’s theorem gives τ (G − e) ≤
2ν(G − e), while τ (G) ≤ τ (G − e) + 1 and ν(G − e) ≤ ν(G). Thus this shortcut yields only
τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G) + 1. Recovering that last unit is the point of the reducible-pair argument
below.
Theorem 1.3. Every graph G with ∆(G) ≤ 7 satisfies τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G).
  Theorem 1.3 assumes only the degree bound; G may be disconnected and its order is
unrestricted. It is deduced in Section 3 from the 7-regular case.
Theorem 1.4. Every 7-regular graph G satisfies τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G).
   The constant 2 cannot be improved inside the class of Theorem 1.3; the extremal exam-
ples are already present at maximum degree three.
Proposition 1.5. K4 has (ν, τ ) = (1, 2) and ∆ = 3; K5 has (ν, τ ) = (2, 4); and for
every k ≥ 1 there are connected graphs G6 , G7 with ∆(G6 ) ≤ 6, ∆(G7 ) = 7, and ν(G6 ) =
ν(G7 ) = k, τ (G6 ) = τ (G7 ) = 2k. Consequently no inequality τ ≤ c ν with c < 2, and no
strict inequality τ < 2ν, holds for all graphs of maximum degree at most 7.
    Proposition 1.5 is proved in Section 11.
1.1. The obstruction at degree seven. Puleo’s proof of Theorem 1.2 is a discharging
argument built on a notion of reducible set (Definition 2.1 below): a vertex set V0 is reducible
if a bounded amount of local packing and covering data lets one delete V0 together with
the edges it interferes with and then recurse. Consequently a minimal counterexample has
no reducible set; our task is to force one from the local structure at degree seven.
   Puleo’s singleton reduction itself has no degree hypothesis. His Lemma 4.4 [8], restated
as Lemma 2.6, makes {v} reducible whenever the link G[N (v)] is weak Kőnig–Egerváry
(WKE). What fails at average degree seven is the discharging step that forces a reducible
configuration from the strict inequality mad(G) < 7 [8, Lemmas 2.7, 2.8]. Reducible pairs
also appear in the literature. Botler, Fernandes and Gutiérrez [2, Lemma 3.3] show that,
in an irreducible robust graph, a pair {x, y} with d(x), d(y) ≤ 6 and |N (x) ∪ N (y)| ≤ 7 can
survive only in a specific configuration: both degrees are five, the common neighbourhood
has order three, and both links are K5 . Such a pair is necessarily non-adjacent [2, Lemma
3.2(b)]. Their configuration therefore differs in two ways from ours: its vertices have degree
at most six, whereas ours have degree seven, and they reduce a non-edge, whereas we reduce
the endpoints of an edge.
   A hypothetical counterexample nevertheless has strong links: each is a connected seven-
vertex graph outside WKE (Lemma 4.4). That condition alone does not make the central
vertex reducible. In K8 every link is K7 , hence connected and outside WKE, but no
                     TUZA’S CONJECTURE FOR MAXIMUM DEGREE SEVEN                              3

singleton of K8 is reducible (Proposition 4.9). Thus the link condition derived from Puleo’s
singleton lemma cannot by itself yield another singleton reduction. We use it instead to
find an edge of high triangle codegree and reduce the two degree-7 endpoints of that edge.
1.2. Outline of the proof. We reduce at an edge of high triangle codegree, where the
triangle codegree c(uv) = |N (u) ∩ N (v)| of an edge is the number of triangles containing it.
Suppose Theorem 1.4 fails and let G be a connected 7-regular graph with τ (G) > 2ν(G).
A short argument about maximum average degree (Lemma 3.1) shows that every proper
subgraph of G falls under Theorem 1.2, so G is minimal in the sense the framework needs
and has no reducible set at all. Then:
    (1) every link G[N (v)] is connected, has seven vertices, and is not in WKE (Lemma 4.4);
    (2) every connected non-WKE graph on seven vertices has at least three vertices of
         degree at least four (Lemma 4.5), so some edge uv of G satisfies c(uv) ≥ 4, while
         7-regularity forces c(uv) ≤ 6 (Corollary 4.7);
    (3) for every edge uv with c(uv) ∈ {4, 5, 6} arising in such a G, the pair {u, v} is
         reducible (Propositions 7.3, 8.5 and 9.1).
   Step (3) contradicts the absence of reducible sets, and Theorem 1.4 follows.
   The last step is finite because a codegree-c edge in a 7-regular graph has a fixed neigh-
bourhood pattern. Writing C = N (u) ∩ N (v) and letting A, B be the exclusive neighbours
of u, v, one has |C| = c and |A| = |B| = 6 − c (Figure 1). All triangles through either
endpoint lie in the resulting local graph, so a local certificate transfers to G. A packing-
and-cover template settles codegrees six and five apart from complete cores, which admit
Fano-plane witnesses. At codegree four, 1,144 admissible local isomorphism classes remain
and are handled by explicit certificates.
   These are among four finite statements verified exhaustively: the seven-vertex link cen-
sus, the two template classifications (including the codegree-five exceptional list), and the
codegree-four catalogue. Everything else is proved in the text. Appendix A describes the
checkers and the precise proof/computation boundary.

                         2. Puleo’s reducibility framework
   We recall the notions and results of [8] that we use, with their exact hypotheses. They
are used as a black box; in particular we do not use Puleo’s discharging lemmas ([8, Lemmas
2.7, 2.8]), whose strict average-degree forcing argument does not supply a configuration at
equality.
Definition 2.1 ([8, Definition 2.1]). When S is a set of triangles, an S-edge is an edge
of some triangle in S. A nonempty set V0 ⊆ V (G) is reducible if there exist a set S of
edge-disjoint triangles in G and a set X of edges of G such that:
     (i) |X| ≤ 2|S|;
    (ii) G − X has no triangle containing a vertex of V0 ; and
   (iii) X contains every S-edge whose endpoints are both outside V0 .
We then say that V0 is reducible using S and X.
 4                                      ANISH GUPTA

  Condition (iii) is easy to overlook but essential: it prevents the recursion from re-using
an edge already spent by S.
Lemma 2.2 ([8, Lemma 2.2]). Let G be a graph and let V0 ⊆ V (G) be reducible using S
and X. Let G′ = (G − X) − V0 . If τ (G′ ) ≤ 2ν(G′ ), then τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G).
Definition 2.3 ([8, Definition 4.2]). A nonempty edge set E0 ⊆ E(G) is reducible if there
exist a set S of edge-disjoint triangles and a set X of edges of G such that (i) |X| ≤ 2|S|;
(ii) G − X has no triangle containing an edge of E0 ; and (iii) X contains every S-edge that
is not in E0 .
Lemma 2.4 ([8, Lemma 4.3]). Let G be a graph and let E0 ⊆ E(G) be reducible using S
and X. Let G′ = (G − X) − E0 . If τ (G′ ) ≤ 2ν(G′ ), then τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G).
Definition 2.5 ([8, Definition 4.1]). A graph H is a weak Kőnig–Egerváry graph if H has
a matching M and a vertex set Q ⊆ V (H) such that |Q| ≤ |M | and Q is a vertex cover in
H − M . We write WKE for the class of such graphs, and say that the pair (M, Q) witnesses
H ∈ WKE.
   Note that M and Q range over all matchings and all vertex sets of the stated size;
in particular M = ∅, Q = ∅ witnesses that every edgeless graph lies in WKE. Every
Kőnig–Egerváry graph, hence every bipartite graph, lies in WKE.
Lemma 2.6 ([8, Lemma 4.4]). Let v ∈ V (G) and let G0 be a nonempty union of components
of G[N (v)]. If G0 ∈ WKE, then G has a reducible set of edges. Also, if G[N (v)] ∈ WKE,
then {v} is reducible.
  For the first claim, Puleo’s proof exhibits the reducible edge set explicitly as E0 = {vw :
w ∈ V (G0 )}.
Corollary 2.7 ([8, Corollary 4.9]). If H is connected and |V (H)| ≤ 4, then H ∈ WKE.
Definition 2.8 ([8, Definition 2.3]). A graph G is robust if for every v ∈ V (G), every
component of G[N (v)] has order at least 5.

                        3. Reduction to the 7-regular case
  The next lemma identifies the equality case in Puleo’s strict hypothesis. Within maxi-
mum degree seven, a connected graph either falls under Theorem 1.2 outright, or is 7-regular
and has all of its proper subgraphs falling under it.
Lemma 3.1. Let K be a connected graph with ∆(K) ≤ 7.
  (a) If K is not 7-regular, then mad(K) < 7.
  (b) If K is 7-regular, then every proper subgraph J ⊊ K satisfies mad(J) < 7.
Proof. Both parts follow from one computation. Suppose L is a nonempty subgraph of K
with 2|E(L)|/|V (L)| ≥ 7, i.e. with average degree at least 7. Every vertex of L has degree
at most ∆(K) ≤ 7 in L, so the average being at least 7 forces every vertex of L to have
degree exactly 7 in L. Fix x ∈ V (L). Then x has 7 neighbours inside L; since x also has
at most 7 neighbours in K, all neighbours of x in K lie in V (L) and all edges of K at x lie
in E(L). As x was arbitrary, V (L) is closed under K-adjacency and E(L) contains every
K-edge incident with V (L). Since K is connected and V (L) ̸= ∅, we get V (L) = V (K)
and E(L) = E(K), that is, L = K.
   For (a): if K is not 7-regular then L = K is impossible, so no such L exists and
mad(K) < 7. For (b): if J ⊊ K is proper and mad(J) ≥ 7, take such an L ⊆ J; then
L = K, so J ⊇ K, contradicting properness. (If E(K) = ∅ the statement is vacuous, since
mad of an edgeless graph is 0.)                                                           □
Proposition 3.2. Theorem 1.4 implies Theorem 1.3.

Proof. Both ν and τ are additive over connected components: every triangle lies in a single
component, the edge sets of distinct components are disjoint, and a union of packings
(respectively transversals) over the components is a packing (respectively transversal) of
the whole graph, optimal if each part is. So it suffices to prove τ (K) ≤ 2ν(K) for every
connected K with ∆(K) ≤ 7.
   If K is 7-regular, this is Theorem 1.4. If not, then mad(K) < 7 by Lemma 3.1(a), and
Theorem 1.2 applies.                                                                     □

           4. The structure of a minimal 7-regular counterexample
  Throughout this section and Sections 5–9 we fix the following.
       Standing hypothesis. G is a connected 7-regular graph with τ (G) >
       2ν(G).
  Such a G exists if Theorem 1.4 fails: a counterexample has a component that is a
counterexample, by additivity, and every component of a 7-regular graph is 7-regular and
connected. Note |V (G)| ≥ 8 and |V (G)| is even.
Lemma 4.1. Every proper subgraph of G satisfies Tuza’s conjecture.
Proof. Immediate from Lemma 3.1(b) and Theorem 1.2.                                      □
Lemma 4.2. G has no reducible vertex set and no reducible edge set.
Proof. Suppose V0 ⊆ V (G) is nonempty and reducible using S and X, and put G′ =
(G − X) − V0 . Since V0 ̸= ∅, V (G′ ) ⊊ V (G), so G′ is a proper subgraph of G and
τ (G′ ) ≤ 2ν(G′ ) by Lemma 4.1. Lemma 2.2 then gives τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G), contradicting the
standing hypothesis.
   Likewise, if E0 ⊆ E(G) is nonempty and reducible using S and X, then G′ = (G−X)−E0
has E(G′ ) ⊊ E(G), so G′ is proper, τ (G′ ) ≤ 2ν(G′ ), and Lemma 2.4 gives the same
contradiction.                                                                      □
Lemma 4.3. G is robust.
Proof. Let v ∈ V (G) and let G0 be a component of G[N (v)] with |V (G0 )| ≤ 4. Then G0
is connected on at most four vertices, so G0 ∈ WKE by Corollary 2.7. By Lemma 2.6 the
edge set E0 = {vw : w ∈ V (G0 )} is reducible; it is nonempty because G0 is a component
of the nonempty graph G[N (v)] (recall d(v) = 7). This contradicts Lemma 4.2.        □
   Lemma 4.3 is [8, Lemma 2.6]; we have repeated its proof to make explicit that the form
of minimality it needs is the one supplied by Lemma 4.1.

vertices with Hv ∈

two components would need at least 10 > 7 vertices, so Hv is connected. If Hv ∈ WKE
then {v} is reducible by Lemma 2.6, contradicting Lemma 4.2.                         □

Corollary 4.7. G has an edge uv with c(uv) ∈ {4, 5, 6}. In fact every vertex of G is
incident with at least three such edges.
Proof. Fix v ∈ V (G) and let Hv = G[N (v)]. For u ∈ N (v) the degree of u inside Hv is
|N (u) ∩ N (v)| = c(uv). By Lemma 4.4, Hv is connected, on seven vertices and not in
WKE, so by Lemma 4.5 at least three of its vertices have degree at least four; that is,
at least three edges uv at v have c(uv) ≥ 4. For the upper bound, if uv ∈ E(G) then
N (u) ∩ N (v) ⊆ N (u) \ {v}, which has 6 elements, so c(uv) ≤ 6.                    □

edge of codegree at least four. Second, the local-transfer lemma allows reducibility of that
edge’s endpoints to be checked in a graph of at most ten vertices. The first step suggests
looking for edge-pair reductions beyond degree seven, and the second remains valid without
change. The finite classifications do not.

Question 12.1. Does mad(G) < 8 imply τ (G) ≤ 2ν(G)?

   Theorem 1.3 settles the maximum-degree-seven portion of the boundary mad(G) ≤ 7,
but not graphs of maximum average degree seven that have vertices of larger degree. The
same first step suggests asking whether the stronger sparsity statement above is tractable.
The finite classifications of Sections 7–9 depend throughout on 7-regularity: through the
degree budget of Lemma 5.5, the identity |A| = |B| = 6−c, and the seven-vertex link census
of Lemma 4.5. Every one of them would have to be redone, and we make no prediction
about whether the method survives.

Question 12.2. Is there a human-readable proof of Proposition 9.1?

   Sections 7 and 8 are structured proofs whose computational content is the verification of
one template inequality over a small explicit family, together with a short exceptional case
settled by a Fano configuration. Section 9 has no comparable structural argument: it is a
catalogue of 1,144 certificates. A conceptual proof of Proposition 9.1 would be the natural
starting point for an attack on Question 12.1.

Question 12.3. Which graphs of maximum degree at most seven satisfy τ = 2ν?

   The planar case has the exact characterization of Cui, Haxell and Ma [3]. It would be
interesting to know what replaces their K4 -based extremal class without planarity, and
in particular how much the K5 blocks in Tuza’s general equality family contribute. In
particular, does any 7-regular graph satisfy τ = 2ν? The finite checks in this paper do not
address that question.

Question 12.4. Does every K5 -free graph satisfy τ ≤ 2ν?

   If G is K5 -free and an edge has at least three common neighbours, then its core G[C] is
triangle-free: a triangle in C, together with the two hubs, would form a K5 . In particular
the two complete cores — the only configurations at codegrees five and six that defeat
the hub-only template — cannot occur. At codegree four it also removes all four core
types containing a triangle, accounting for 364 of the 1,144 catalogued orbits. Whether
that observation can replace the degree hypothesis is unclear. The stronger restriction to
K4 -free graphs is itself unresolved in general; work of Munaro treats several subclasses and
shows that the factor two would remain essentially tight even there [7].
   Tuza’s conjecture remains open, and Theorem 1.3 does not improve Haxell’s universal
bound τ ≤ (66/23) ν [4]. Its narrower point is that the equality boundary of Puleo’s sparsity
theorem can be crossed, which motivates Question 12.1.
